q325.question: What did Jesus teach Nathaniel about angels on the way to Bethany?
q325.answer:
On the hill road going up from Jericho to Bethany, Nathaniel asked Jesus what they should teach the people about the heavenly ministers, since the high priest and the other Sadducees did not believe in angels [167:7.1]. Jesus' reply is the most orderly teaching about angels that he left during his earth life, setting out in turn what angels are, what they do not do, and what they do for man [167:7.2-7.6].

The main point is that angels are an order of creatures wholly different from man, and that they are not God's watchers but spirit ministers who serve man and link the worlds together.

1. Angels Are Beings Created Separately, Different from Man

Jesus said that the angelic hosts are a separate order of created beings, entirely different from the material order of mortal creatures, and that they function as a distinct group of universe intelligences [167:7.2]. Angels do not belong to the group called "⟦Q 167:7.2⟧the Sons of God⟦/Q⟧" in the Scriptures, nor are they the glorified spirits of mortals who have progressed through the mansion worlds [167:7.2]. Angels are a direct creation; they do not reproduce themselves, and they have only a spiritual kinship with the human race [167:7.2]. So Jesus made it clear that, although ascending man does at one time traverse a state of being analogous to that of the angels, "⟦Q 167:7.2⟧mortal man never becomes an angel⟦/Q⟧" [167:7.2]. These words correct the common idea that people who die become angels.

2. The Nature of Angels: Immortal but Neither All-Knowing nor All-Powerful

Angels are immortal beings who do not die as men do, except for those who become involved in sin, as did some who were caught up in the deceptions of Lucifer [167:7.3]. As the spirit ministers of heaven they are neither all-wise nor all-powerful, and all the loyal angels are truly pure and holy [167:7.3]. The teaching is that angels are not to be revered as gods but seen as holy fellow servants who share in the work of God.

3. Angels Are Not Spying Watchers but Ministers Who Link the Worlds

Jesus said that angels are not spies of the spirit world who watch men and then go to tell the Father the thoughts of their hearts and report on the deeds of the flesh. The Father has no need of such service, since his own spirit lives within man [167:7.4]. Rather, the angels work to keep one world in touch with other worlds and to let one part of creation know about the affairs of other, distant parts [167:7.4]. And many angels are assigned to the service of the human race; Jesus stressed that the saying that seraphim are "ministering spirits" is neither figurative nor poetic but a fact [167:7.4].

4. The Work of Saving Men and Guidance after Death

Many angels are engaged in the work of saving men, and there is seraphic joy when a soul forsakes sin and begins to seek God [167:7.5]. The saying that there is joy in the presence of the angels of heaven over one sinner who repents also points to the existence of higher orders of celestial beings concerned with the spiritual progress of mortals [167:7.5]. The angels are also much concerned with conducting the souls of men to the mansion worlds, acting as sure guides of the soul during the indeterminate period between the death of the flesh and the new life [167:7.6]. As explained elsewhere, the guardian seraphim are the custodial trustees of the survival values of the sleeping soul, and in the resurrection halls they co-operate with the Adjuster to help reassemble the personality [113:6.5]. That is why it is said that "⟦Q 113:6.6⟧the guardian seraphim will repersonalize you⟦/Q⟧" [113:6.6].

5. What It Means for Our Life of Faith

Jesus said that these matters, though hard to understand, are all true [167:7.4]. One who knows the ministry of angels does not think he needs an intermediary between himself and God. The Father dwells directly within us by his spirit [167:7.4], and the angels are ministers who walk that road with us. It is a great comfort that even on a path of faith that seems to be walked alone, many unseen companions rejoice and go along with us [167:7.5].

Summary

According to Jesus, angels are immortal spirit ministers directly created as an order different from man, and people do not die and become angels [167:7.2, 167:7.3]. Angels are not watchers on the Father's behalf but beings who link the worlds, serve man, and share in the joy of salvation [167:7.4, 167:7.5], and they even take on the work of guiding and guarding the soul between death and resurrection [167:7.6, 113:6.5].

q326.question: How did the resurrection of Lazarus take place, and what is its significance compared with Jesus' other miracles?
q326.answer:
The Urantia Book calls the raising of Lazarus at Bethany the greatest of all the events connected with the earth ministry of Michael of Nebadon, the supreme manifestation of divine power during his incarnation [168:1.9]. Since Jesus' own resurrection came after he had been delivered from the bonds of mortal flesh, this means that the resurrection of Lazarus was the high point of the power he showed while clothed in the flesh [168:1.9].

This event was the work of a vast celestial organization moving behind the visible stage, and its outcome fostered hostility as well as faith, hastening Jesus' death.

1. Unseen Preparation: The Holding of the Adjuster and the Celestial Host

According to the universe records, Jesus' Personalized Adjuster issued orders, just fifteen minutes before Lazarus drew his last breath, to hold Lazarus's Thought Adjuster on this planet indefinitely [168:1.6]. As to whether the divine mind of Jesus knew beforehand that he would raise him, the authors honestly say they do not know [168:1.7]. The little group gathered before the tomb did not know that, under the direction of Gabriel, celestial beings of every order were waiting close at hand for the word of command [168:1.10].

2. What Actually Happened: Revival in Twelve Seconds

After offering a prayer of thanksgiving to the Father, Jesus called to Lazarus with a loud voice [168:2.2]. Then the celestial host moved in unified action, and "⟦Q 168:2.3⟧In just twelve seconds of earth time⟦/Q⟧" [168:2.3] the lifeless form stirred and sat up. When Lazarus came forth, Jesus' Personalized Adjuster commanded Lazarus's former Adjuster, which had been waiting, to return to the mind and soul of the resurrected man [168:2.6]. Lazarus remembered only falling asleep and waking up, for time does not exist for those who sleep the sleep of death [168:2.9].

3. Why It Is Unique: The First and Last on Urantia

This resurrection restored a mortal in his very fleshly form, which was far more difficult than the usual technique of resurrecting mortals in morontia form and required more celestial personalities and much more universe equipment [168:1.11]. Gabriel left on record that this event, in which Lazarus was resurrected in the likeness of his mortal body of death, was the first and last of its kind on Urantia [168:2.8]. Moreover, because the Jews believed that the soul lingered by the tomb only until the end of the third day, a revival after four days had passed became a genuine case that no one could deny [168:1.14, 168:1.15]. Jesus told Lazarus that all who believe the gospel would experience the same thing, but would be resurrected in a more glorious form [168:2.7].

4. Jesus' Tears and Hesitation

As to why Jesus wept, the authors point to his deep sympathy for the sisters, his discomfort at the outward show of mourning, and his hesitation at having to call his friend back into bitter persecution [168:1.2-1.5]. It shows that the one who worked the miracle was a man who felt both love and pain.

5. The Consequences

Many believed, but others hardened their hearts all the more [168:2.10], and the Sanhedrin formally decided to put Jesus to death without a trial [168:3.2]. Lazarus too was threatened with death; he fled to Philadelphia, became treasurer of the church there, and died at the age of sixty-seven of the same sickness as before [168:5.1-5.3].

Summary

The resurrection of Lazarus was a once-only revival in the very flesh, brought about by the holding of the Adjuster and the co-operation of the celestial host under Gabriel [168:1.6, 168:1.10, 168:2.8]. It was the supreme manifestation of Michael's power in the flesh [168:1.9] and a living proof of the promise that believers will be resurrected in a more glorious form [168:2.7], but at the same time it became the occasion that hastened the decision to kill Jesus [168:3.1].

q327.question: When Lazarus died even though Jesus had said "this sickness is not unto death," what did Jesus teach about the answering of prayer?
q327.answer:
The apostles were greatly perplexed that Lazarus had actually died even though Jesus had sent word that "this sickness is not to the death," and on the way from Bethany to Pella they asked him again and again about prayer and its answers [168:4.2]. Jesus' answer is summarized in ten points [168:4.3], and its core is that sincere prayer is always answered, but the answer comes in spiritual form according to God's wisdom and the conditions of time and space, sometimes greatly delayed.

In fact, when Jesus sent that message, Lazarus had already been dead eleven hours [168:4.5]. The promise was not false; it was only delayed for the sake of a better answer.

1. Prayer Is the Effort of the Finite to Approach the Infinite

Because prayer is the expression of the finite mind in an effort to approach the Infinite, prayer is limited by the knowledge of the finite, and the answer is conditioned by the vision and purposes of the Infinite [168:4.4]. Therefore no visible material continuity is ever observed between a prayer and its spiritual answer [168:4.4].

2. Delay Is Not Refusal

The delay of an apparently unanswered prayer often betokens a better answer [168:4.5]. Jesus said that "⟦Q 168:4.5⟧No sincere prayer is denied an answer⟦/Q⟧" [168:4.5], except that at times the superior viewpoint of the spiritual world devises an answer that meets the petition of the spirit rather than the prayer of the mere mind of man [168:4.5]. Some prayers are so vast and all-embracing that they can be received only in eternity, even on Paradise [168:4.6]. And some answers can be recognized only when the mind that prayed has attained the immortal state or the spirit level [168:4.7].

3. Prayer Is Addressed to Spiritual Beings and Answered Spiritually

All true prayer is addressed to spiritual beings and answered in spiritual terms; spirit beings cannot bestow material answers even to the spirit petitions of material beings [168:4.9]. Prayers distorted by ignorance and superstition are translated by the intervening spirit beings, so that the one who prays may not recognize the answer when it comes [168:4.8]. And no prayer can hope for an answer unless it is born of the spirit and fostered by faith [168:4.10].

4. Faith Leaves the Manner of the Answer to God

Sincere faith implies that one has in advance granted those who hear the prayer the full right to answer it in accordance with their supreme wisdom and divine love [168:4.10]. It is always right for a child to ask of a parent, and it is also within the parent's duty, by higher wisdom, to delay, modify, or postpone the answer to another stage of spiritual ascension [168:4.11].

5. Ask without Hesitation, but Remember Time

Jesus said not to hesitate to pray prayers of spirit longing. The answer is held in trust, awaiting our attainment of the future spiritual level at which we can recognize it [168:4.12]. "⟦Q 168:4.13⟧Todas las solicitudes nacidas genuinamente del espíritu tendrán, con certeza, respuesta.⟦/Q⟧" [168:4.13]. But since we are progressive creatures of time and space, we must constantly reckon with the time-space factor in our experience of receiving the full answer [168:4.13]. This teaching leads us to see prayer not as a tool for moving God but as an expression of faith that leaves the outcome to the Father [168:4.10, 168:4.11].

Summary

The case of Lazarus shows that the answer to prayer can come in a form and at a time different from what man expects [168:4.2, 168:4.5]. Sincere, spirit-born prayer is never denied, but the answer is received in spiritual form, according to God's wisdom, and sometimes only in the next world [168:4.6, 168:4.9, 168:4.12]. Faith, then, is not dictating the result but entrusting the manner of the answer to the loving Father [168:4.10, 168:4.11].

q328.question: What do the three parables of the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son each teach?
q328.answer:
Preaching on "⟦Q 169:1.1⟧the grace of salvation⟦/Q⟧" at Pella, Jesus retold the stories of the lost sheep and the lost coin and then added his favorite parable, that of the prodigal son [169:1.1]. The common theme of the three stories is that while man is seeking God, God is also seeking man [169:1.2]. Yet the three also show different ways in which people get lost, and the Father's different kinds of love suited to each [169:1.15].

Jesus liked to tell these three stories together, and The Urantia Book itself sums up the meaning of each [169:1.15].

1. The Lost Sheep: Those Who Go Astray Unintentionally

A sheep goes astray unintentionally [169:1.4]. This story shows that when people unintentionally go astray from the way of life, the Father is mindful of them and goes out, with his Sons, the true shepherds of the flock, to seek them [169:1.15]. Jesus said that the fact that souls are lost only increases the interest of the Father in heaven [169:1.2]. Going further, he said that "⟦Q 169:1.3⟧the Father accepts you even before you have repented⟦/Q⟧" [169:1.3], overturning the old teaching that acceptance comes only after sacrifice and penitence have been paid.

2. The Lost Coin: Those Blinded and Buried under the Cares of the World

A coin is covered over by the dust of the years and hidden by the accumulation of men's belongings [169:1.4]. This story shows the thoroughness of the divine search for those who are confused, or spiritually blinded, by the material cares and accumulations of life [169:1.15]. As the woman lights a lamp and diligently sweeps the house, so the Father and the Son use every influence that can help in finding the lost [169:1.4]. The sheep is lost in the wilderness, but the coin is lost right inside the house, so when the Son of Man goes out into the wilderness he also seeks the coin lost in the house [169:1.4].

3. The Lost Son: Those Who Leave Deliberately, and Complete Restoration

The sheep went astray without knowing it, but the young man left home deliberately [169:1.5]. Only after he had wasted his inheritance in riotous living and was reduced to feeding swine did he come to himself and resolve to go back [169:1.7, 169:1.8]. All the while the father had sorrowed much over his son and was always waiting for his return [169:1.9]. And while the son was still a long way off, the father ran out and embraced him, and before the son had even finished his confession he had the best robe and the son's ring brought [169:1.9]. This parable shows that the Father completely restores the lost son to the Father's house and heart [169:1.15]. The request to be taken on even as a hired servant never needed to be spoken at all.

4. The Elder Son: One Who Stayed Near Yet Could Not Rejoice

The latter part of the parable portrays the elder son, faithful but self-centered and full of self-satisfaction [169:1.6]. Resenting the feast for his brother, he would not go in [169:1.12], and the father reasoned with him: "⟦Q 169:1.13⟧you have all the while been with me, and all this which I have is yours⟦/Q⟧" [169:1.13]. It is emphasized that the father truly loved both of his sons [169:1.13]. It is a warning that even one who has lived righteously can distance himself from the Father's joy if he regards grace as a reward for merit.

Summary

The three parables show the Father's love seeking and recovering, respectively, the one who strays unintentionally, the one buried under the cares of the world, and the one who leaves deliberately [169:1.4, 169:1.5, 169:1.15]. The Father accepts us even before we repent [169:1.3] and fully restores those who return to the place of sons [169:1.9], and this story of the prodigal, together with that of the good Samaritan, was Jesus' favorite way of teaching the love of the Father [169:1.14, 169:1.16].

q329.question: What is the "kingdom of heaven" Jesus spoke of, and how differently did the apostles and the later church understand it?
q329.answer:
The kingdom of heaven Jesus spoke of is not a political state or an institution to be suddenly set up at the end of the world; it is a spiritual experience and brotherhood founded on the truths of the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man [170:2.1]. Jesus strove to turn this concept into the ideal of "⟦Q 170:2.11⟧doing the will of God⟦/Q⟧" [170:2.11], and he sought to use, instead of kingdom, king, and subjects, the concepts of the heavenly family, the heavenly Father, and the liberated sons of God engaged in joyful service [170:2.12].

But this concept was hard even for the apostles, and in later times the institution of the church took the place of the kingdom.

1. Jesus' Kingdom: A Spiritual Experience Founded on the Fatherhood and the Brotherhood

Jesus said that by accepting this teaching man is delivered from his age-old animal fears and gains new courage and spiritual power, comfort reaching even to the poor, new standards of morality, the supremacy of the spiritual, and spiritual attainment as the goal of life [170:2.1-2.6]. What is needed to enter the kingdom is childlike faith and sincerity, and a hunger for righteousness [170:2.20-2.22]. Jesus also called the kingdom "⟦Q 170:2.24⟧family fellowship with God the Father⟦/Q⟧" [170:2.24], and he never once called the Father a king [169:4.1].

2. The Two Stages and Five Phases of the Kingdom

Jesus taught the twofold nature of the kingdom: on the one hand, the supreme desire to do the will of God in this world together with unselfish love, and on the other, the kingdom in heaven, where love for God is perfected [170:2.17-2.19]. In one sermon he also pointed to five phases: the personal inward experience, the enlarged brotherhood of believers, the brotherhood of invisible spirit beings, the dawn of a new social order, and the age of light and life [170:4.1-4.6]. So when Jesus speaks of the kingdom, we must always notice which phase he means [170:4.7].

3. The Apostles' Understanding: Between Inner Experience and a Dramatic Future Event

The apostles saw the kingdom as a personal experience in the heart, yet at the same time they regarded it as a world event to come suddenly and dramatically in the future [170:2.13-2.16]. In particular, the expectation that Jesus would soon return in power and glory to set up the kingdom seeped even into the gospel records, but Jesus did not connect the establishment of the kingdom with his return to this world [170:2.10, 170:4.15]. Because the disciples hastily bound the two promises together, generations lived on disappointed hopes [170:4.16].

4. The Later Church's Understanding: The Institution Takes the Place of the Kingdom

Jewish believers believed that Jesus would soon return to set up a more or less material kingdom, while Gentile Christians, following Paul's doctrines, came to see Jesus as the redeemer of the children of the church [170:5.5, 170:5.6]. The Urantia Book says that the rise of the church as a social outgrowth of the kingdom was in itself natural and even desirable, yet it points out that "⟦Q 170:5.7⟧The evil of the church was not its existence⟦/Q⟧" [170:5.7], but that it almost completely supplanted Jesus' concept of the kingdom [170:5.7].

5. What It Means for Us Today

We are warned not to be discouraged even if the progress of the kingdom seems slow, and above all not to make the fatal mistake of failing to establish it in our own souls while looking for its outward, age-long manifestations [170:4.14]. The gospel of the kingdom emphasizes the pre-eminence of the individual, the will as the determining factor, spiritual fellowship with the Father, the satisfactions of loving service, and the transcendency of the spiritual [170:4.8-4.13].

Summary

The kingdom of heaven is a spiritual experience and brotherhood of doing the will of God, founded on the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man [170:2.1, 170:2.11]. The apostles understood it as bound up with a dramatic future event, especially the second coming [170:4.16], and the later church replaced it with an institution [170:5.7], but the kingdom Jesus desired begins with God's rule in the heart of each person who enters now by faith [170:2.20, 170:4.2].

q330.question: Why did Jesus, a man of peace, drive the traders out of the temple, and what does this event teach us?
q330.answer:
The cleansing of the temple was not a sudden outburst by Jesus because he could not hold back his anger; it was an event that revealed his deep detestation of the injustice of commercializing religion and exploiting the poor [173:1.11]. The Urantia Book explains that this took place on Monday morning, the day after the entry into Jerusalem [173:1.10], and that the confusion and injustice going on in the very place where Jesus intended to teach aroused in his soul those emotions of indignation that came to him periodically [173:1.5, 173:1.6].

To understand this event, we must first see what was going on in the temple courts at that time.

1. Commerce and Exploitation in the Temple Courts

Because sacrificial animals had to be "without blemish," the animals worshipers brought were often rejected by the inspectors, and so the custom of buying sacrifices in the temple courts became fixed, and enormous profits flowed to the families of the high priests [173:1.1]. These commercial markets were maintained until they were destroyed by a mob three years before the temple itself was destroyed [173:1.2]. Greedy priests even demanded the price of a week's labor for a pair of doves that should have sold for a few pennies [173:1.2]. Also, because the temple tax had to be paid in Jewish coin, money-changers set up tables in the temple courts and charged high fees [173:1.3]. Great sums piled up in the temple treasury, while "⟦Q 173:1.4⟧the common people languished in poverty and continued to pay these unjust levies⟦/Q⟧" [173:1.4].

2. What Happened That Morning

Just as Jesus was about to begin his discourse, a quarrel broke out at a money-changer's table over the overcharging of a Jew from Alexandria, a drove of some one hundred bullocks went bellowing by, and a humble Galilean was being jeered at and jostled by arrogant Judeans [173:1.6]. Jesus was not the only one angered by such desecration; the common people and the pilgrims from foreign lands were also sincerely indignant [173:1.5]. At that very hour the Sanhedrin too was holding its meeting in a chamber surrounded by this commercial din and confusion [173:1.5].

3. What Actually Took Place

Jesus took a whip of cords from a lad who was driving the animals, drove the animals out of the temple, and opened the doors of all the pens [173:1.7]. It was the thrilled pilgrims who overturned the tables, and in less than five minutes the commercial activity of the temple had been swept away [173:1.7]. Jesus returned to the platform and, quoting the Scriptures, said that the house of prayer for all nations had been made a den of robbers [173:1.7]. For that whole day the temple courts were quiet and peaceful, and the people hung on his every word [173:1.9]. The chief priests, on the other hand, became all the more determined to destroy him [173:1.9]. The apostles were so astonished by this sudden action that they did not lift a hand [173:1.10].

4. What This Event Teaches

The Urantia Book says that this event shows two things. The first is Jesus' attitude toward commercializing the practices of religion and toward all exploitation at the expense of the poor and the unlearned [173:1.11]. The second is that Jesus did not look with approval upon the refusal to use force to protect the majority when an unjust minority hides behind political, financial, or ecclesiastical power to oppress them [173:1.11]. Therefore it says that "⟦Q 173:1.11⟧Shrewd, wicked, and designing men⟦/Q⟧" [173:1.11] are not to be permitted to organize themselves to exploit idealists.

Summary

The cleansing of the temple was Jesus' righteous action against the commercialization of religion, which had turned the house of worship into a market of profiteering, and against the exploitation of the poor [173:1.1-1.4, 173:1.11]. It was a moment of indignation, but its result was order and peaceful teaching [173:1.9], and today it teaches us the lesson that faith must not be indifferent in the face of injustice [173:1.11].

q331.question: Does God forgive us before we repent, or after repentance and confession?
q331.answer:
This is the very question that Peter and James brought to Jesus. James held that the Father forgives us even before we ask, while Peter maintained that repentance and confession must precede forgiveness [174:1.1]. Jesus' answer was not to choose one of the two. He said that both of them were mistaken because they failed to understand the nature of the intimate and loving relationship between the creature and the Creator [174:1.2].

The core is that on God's side forgiveness is already inherent, and that what is needed on man's side is the capacity of the soul to receive that forgiveness.

1. The Illustration of the Wise Parent

Jesus said that it is doubtful whether an intelligent and affectionate parent would ever have to forgive a normal child [174:1.2]. For an understanding relationship joined with love forestalls in advance the estrangement that would later need the readjustment of repentance and forgiveness [174:1.2]. A parent views the immaturity of the child in the light of riper experience, and the heavenly Father possesses this capacity for sympathy and understanding infinitely [174:1.3].

2. Divine Forgiveness Is Inherent and Inevitable

Jesus said that "⟦Q 174:1.3⟧Divine forgiveness is inevitable⟦/Q⟧" [174:1.3], inherent and inalienable in God's infinite understanding and his perfect knowledge of the child's mistaken choosing [174:1.3]. And divine justice is so eternally fair that it always embodies understanding mercy [174:1.3]. Elsewhere, too, Jesus taught that God has already forgiven sin [170:2.23]. The teaching of the parable of the prodigal son, that the Father accepts us even before we have repented, means the same thing [169:1.3]. Whereas Moses taught the dignity and justice of a Creator God, Jesus portrayed the love and mercy of a heavenly Father [188:4.4]. Even on the cross he asked the Father to forgive his executioners [187:2.4].

3. The Sense of Separation Lies in Man's Consciousness

Why, then, does man feel guilt and estrangement? Being immature, the child often feels a guilty sense of separation from the father's approval, but the true father is never conscious of any such separation [174:1.4]. Jesus said: "⟦Q 174:1.4⟧El pecado es una experiencia de la conciencia de la criatura; no es parte de la conciencia de Dios.⟦/Q⟧." [174:1.4] Repentance and confession are not conditions that change God's mind; they are the process by which man goes beyond the sense of separation on his own side and returns to a love that is already there. So the concern of the true believer is not with future punishment but with present separation from God [188:4.10].

4. The Way to Receive Forgiveness: Forgiving Others

Jesus taught that the way to receive God's forgiveness personally is the act of forgiving one's fellows. When we forgive our brethren in the flesh, we create the capacity in our own souls for receiving God's forgiveness of our own misdeeds [170:2.23]. When we understand the inner impulses of our fellows we will love them, and when we love our brother we have already forgiven him [174:1.4]. Conversely, the inability to forgive is the measure of immaturity, and resentment and vengefulness are in direct proportion to ignorance of the other's inner nature [174:1.5]. Jesus added that love is the outworking of the divine and inner urge of life, founded on understanding, nurtured by unselfish service, and perfected in wisdom [174:1.5]. Therefore the path of forgiveness begins with the effort to understand the other more deeply.

Summary

God's forgiveness is not a conditional bargain that waits on repentance; it is inherent in his infinite understanding and love [174:1.3]. Guilty separation is only an experience in man's consciousness [174:1.4], and by understanding and forgiving our brothers we cultivate in our souls the capacity to receive God's forgiveness, which is already given [170:2.23, 174:1.5].

q332.question: Jesus promised to come again; how does The Urantia Book explain the second coming of Christ?
q332.answer:
The Urantia Book acknowledges the fact that Jesus clearly promised that he would sometime return in person to this world [176:4.3]. But it explains that he did not say how, where, or when he would come, and that binding his return to particular events such as the destruction of Jerusalem or the end of the world was the disciples' interpretation [176:4.2, 176:4.6]. It says that this promise of a second coming is the most misunderstood part of the Master's teaching [176:4.1].

The Urantia Book's account of the second coming honestly separates what is certain from what cannot be known.

1. The Two Things Jesus Actually Promised

Jesus promised to do two things after his ascension. The first was to send another teacher, the Spirit of Truth, which was fulfilled at Pentecost [176:4.3]. The second was to return in person to this world at some time [176:4.3]. On the Mount of Olives he said, "⟦Q 176:2.3⟧I also promise that I will sometime return to this world⟦/Q⟧" [176:2.3], adding that in the meantime the Spirit of Truth would comfort and guide them [176:2.3]. He also intimated that when he returned he would come in power and in spirit, and that only the eyes of the spirit would discern him [176:2.4].

2. Why the Misunderstanding Arose

The disciples did not hesitate to connect the prediction of the destruction of Jerusalem with the promise of his return, and they interpreted it so even though Jesus tried to correct that misunderstanding [176:2.2]. Jesus said rather that the things now seen were coming to an end, but that this would be a new beginning out of which the gospel of the kingdom would go to all the world [176:2.3]. When the Master did not appear even after the Roman armies destroyed the temple, his followers came to associate his return with the end of the age, and even with the end of the world [176:4.2]. Moreover, the teaching of this evening became the most confusedly distorted of all the gospel records; a Jewish apocalypse written by a man named Selta was carried over into the Gospel of Matthew, and the parable of the ten virgins first appeared in that writing [176:2.8].

3. What Is Known and What Is Not

The time of his return is known only in the councils of Paradise; not even the angels of heaven know it [176:2.5]. The revelators themselves confess that they firmly believe Michael will come again, but that they have no idea when or how he will come [176:4.5]. They think it likely, however, that the whole world will know of it, since he will come not as an obscure babe but as the supreme ruler of a universe [176:4.5]. They also express the view that he who bears the title of Planetary Prince of Urantia will visit many times in future ages [176:4.4]. Therefore they advise: "⟦Q 176:4.6⟧Por lo tanto haríais bien en desasociar el retorno personal del Maestro a la tierra de todo evento establecido o época fijada.⟦/Q⟧" [176:4.6].

4. The "Second Coming" That Comes to Each Person

Jesus applied the meaning of the teaching about the coming of the Sons of God to the individual. Each person, on passing through the portals of death, comes at once to judgment and faces a new dispensation of service [176:2.7]. Thus the second coming has no more special meaning for human beings than the ordinary event of natural death, and natural death leads us directly into the events that bring us into the presence of Jesus, the sovereign of the universe [176:4.7]. As he stands ready to receive us in heaven, so we on earth must always be ready to welcome him [176:4.7].

Summary

Jesus made the promise to send the Spirit of Truth and the promise to return in person, and the first was fulfilled at Pentecost [176:4.3]. The second promise is certain, but no one knows its time or manner, and binding it to the destruction of Jerusalem or the end of the world was the disciples' misunderstanding [176:2.2, 176:4.5, 176:4.6]. What matters for us is not calculating dates but living always ready to welcome him [176:2.7, 176:4.7].

q333.question: Why was Jesus almost silent before the Sanhedrin, and in what ways did that trial violate even Jewish law?
q333.answer:
After his arrest Jesus was taken first to Annas and then before the members of the Sanhedrin gathered in the palace of the high priest Caiaphas. The Urantia Book says that this whole proceeding was irregular and entirely contrary to Jewish law [184:5.6]. And there Jesus said not a word in reply to the false testimony, yet he answered at once and clearly the one question that concerned his bestowal mission [184:3.6, 184:3.16]. His silence was not helplessness but the strongest answer truth could give in the face of falsehood.

Let us look in turn at the course of the trial, its illegality, and the meaning of the silence.

1. The Examination before Annas

Annas, grown rich from the temple revenues, was the most powerful man in all Jewish society, and he wanted the trial of Jesus to remain in the hands of the Sadducees [184:1.1]. At first he thought he could persuade Jesus to recant his claims and leave Palestine, but before the dignified and composed Jesus he realized that this was useless [184:1.2]. The threat to his revenues from the cleansing of the temple fed his hostility more than the teaching did [184:1.3]. Jesus did not answer when asked for the names of his disciples, and said that since he had taught openly and without concealment, Annas should ask those who had heard him [184:1.4, 184:1.6]. Yet he asked Annas kindly how, knowing what he was doing, he could reject the light of God [184:1.5].

2. The "Trial" before Caiaphas

The court that Caiaphas convened at half past three on Friday morning was not a regular session of the Sanhedrin; it was a gathering of about thirty members in the high priest's palace, not in the appointed place [184:3.1, 184:3.2]. The Sanhedrin had already three times voted his death [184:3.1]. Ordinarily capital cases were handled with great care, but this time Caiaphas was more a prosecutor than an impartial judge [184:3.4]. The testimony of more than twenty false witnesses was so contradictory that even the members were ashamed [184:3.6].

3. Ways in Which It Violated Jewish Law

Jewish law required that at least two witnesses agree on the same point, and it forbade the testimony of a traitor [184:3.6]. But apart from the saying about raising the temple in three days, no two witnesses ever agreed on any matter, and even that was not exactly what Jesus had said, nor was he given any opportunity to explain [184:3.7, 184:5.6]. A death sentence required two sessions, with a day of fasting and mourning between them, but they waited only one hour [184:4.1]. No formal vote was taken even on the charge of blasphemy [184:5.7], and the three charges to be laid before Pilate were settled without hearing any testimony and in the absence of the accused [184:5.2-5.5, 184:5.8]. At this, three Pharisees left so as not to take part [184:5.8].

4. Silence and a Single Answer

Throughout the false accusations Jesus did not open his mouth, and the testimony, full of hatred and exaggeration, fell in its own entanglements. "⟦Q 184:3.8⟧The very best refutation of their false accusations was the Master's calm and majestic silence⟦/Q⟧." [184:3.8] But when Caiaphas asked him, in the name of the living God, whether he was the Son of God, Jesus answered that he was, and said that he would soon go to the Father [184:3.14]. Then the high priest tore his garments and cried blasphemy, and all cried out that he should be put to death [184:3.15]. During the hour that followed, the guards and servants mocked and struck him, and Jesus sent John away so that he would not lose his life through his indignation [184:4.1, 184:4.2].

5. Victory in Humiliation

The Urantia Book calls these moments the moments of the greatest triumph of the Master's whole life [184:4.6]. He did not defend himself, but he was not defenseless; he was not conquered, he simply did not fight in the material sense [184:4.5]. He who had been revealing God to man was now revealing man to God [184:4.6]. "⟦Q 184:3.19⟧Man sits in judgment on God, but even then he loves them⟦/Q⟧" [184:3.19] and would save them if he could.

Summary

The Sanhedrin trial was an illegal proceeding: it was not a regular session, it violated the rules on witnesses and on two sessions, and it framed charges without the accused present [184:3.2, 184:4.1, 184:5.6, 184:5.8]. Jesus answered falsehood with silence and the question about his mission with a clear affirmation [184:3.8, 184:3.16], and his attitude of loving his judges even in humiliation was his greatest victory [184:3.19, 184:4.6].

q334.question: What was the meaning of Jesus' washing of feet and his establishing of the remembrance supper at the Last Supper?
q334.answer:
At the Last Supper Jesus performed two symbolic acts. One was washing the apostles' feet, and the other was establishing the remembrance supper with the cup and the bread. The foot washing was a parable illustrating the new commandment he was about to give, the love of serving one another [179:3.6], and the remembrance supper was the symbol of a new dispensation replacing the old Passover and a symbolic meeting of the believer with Michael [179:5.2, 179:5.6].

Both acts were meant to teach love and spiritual freedom rather than form and doctrine.

1. The Foot Washing: To Apostles Who Had Quarreled over the Places of Honor

That night the apostles had not only proudly refused to wash one another's feet but had even quarreled over who would have the places of honor at the table [179:3.9]. Jesus silently rose, went to where the water pitcher, basin, and towels were, and knelt at the apostles' feet [179:3.1, 179:3.5], and when Peter said he must never do so, Jesus told him that if his feet were not washed he would have no part in what Jesus was about to do [179:3.3, 179:3.5]. He went around the table washing the feet of all twelve apostles, "⟦Q 179:3.7⟧not even passing by Judas⟦/Q⟧" [179:3.7]. Then he asked why, when their Master had washed their feet, they had been unwilling to wash one another's feet, and taught that a servant is not greater than his master [179:3.8]. Jesus said that at his table there could be no places of preferment, and that he loved each one as he loved the others [179:3.9].

2. The Remembrance Supper: The Meaning of the Cup and the Bread

Jesus took up the third cup, "⟦Q 179:5.1⟧the cup of blessing⟦/Q⟧," and said that this was the cup of his remembrance, the cup of the blessing of a new dispensation of grace and truth, the emblem of the bestowal and ministry of the Spirit of Truth [179:5.1]. Then, breaking the bread, he said: "⟦Q 179:5.3⟧El verbo del Padre, tal como es revelado en el Hijo, es en verdad el pan de la vida».⟦/Q⟧." [179:5.3] The bread of remembrance is the symbol of the living word of truth incarnated in the likeness of mortal flesh [179:5.3]. Whereas the old Passover commemorated the coming out of bondage into freedom, the new supper symbolizes the passing out of the bondage of ceremonialism and selfishness into the brotherhood of the liberated sons of faith [179:5.2].

3. Why He Left It Only as a Symbol

Jesus deliberately used symbols so that his successors would find it difficult to attach precise interpretations to them. He sought to prevent later generations from binding his teaching with the dead chains of tradition and dogma, and he did not wish to suppress the spiritual imagination of the believer [179:5.4]. But later people turned this simple symbol into a formula of almost mathematical precision, and of all Jesus' teachings none has been so standardized by tradition [179:5.5]. This supper was instituted in a friend's upper room, without the sanction of a church, without sacred forms or ceremonial consecration [179:5.8].

4. For Those Who Take Part in the Remembrance Supper

When those who believe in the Son and know God take part, the Master is really present, and his spirit fraternizes with the indwelling fragment of the Father [179:5.6]. Jesus said that when they do this they should first recall his life in the flesh and then discern by faith that they will sometime sup with him in the Father's eternal kingdom [179:5.9]. And he said that the new Passover he was leaving them was the memory of his bestowal life, the word of eternal truth, and the Spirit of Truth to be poured out upon all flesh [179:5.9]. He also urged them not to dispute over who is greatest but to be all as brothers [179:5.7].

Summary

The foot washing was an enacted parable teaching the love of mutual service in place of strife over rank [179:3.6, 179:3.8], and the remembrance supper was a new Passover in memory of Jesus' life, the word of truth, and the Spirit of Truth [179:5.1, 179:5.9]. Jesus left it only as a symbol so that it would not be locked into forms, and he is really present to those who take part in faith [179:5.4, 179:5.6].

q335.question: How does the new commandment, "love one another even as I have loved you," differ from the old commandment to love one's neighbor?
q335.answer:
In his farewell discourse Jesus told the apostles, who well knew the commandment "⟦Q 180:1.1⟧love your neighbor even as yourself⟦/Q⟧," that he was not wholly satisfied with even that sincere devotion [180:1.1]. And he gave them a new commandment: "⟦Q 180:1.1⟧Que os améis los unos a los otros así como yo os he amado.⟦/Q⟧" [180:1.1]. If the standard of the old commandment is "myself," the standard of the new commandment is "⟦Q 188:5.2⟧the love of Jesus⟦/Q⟧." The measure of love has been raised from self-love to the love shown by the Son of God.

This commandment was first enacted just before, in the foot washing. While washing their feet, Jesus said that he was performing this service as a parable illustrating the meaning of the new commandment he was about to give [179:3.6].

1. The Measure of Love Has Changed

Jesus said that by this commandment he was setting up the supreme measure of true affection, and that there is no greater love than to lay down one's life for one's friends [180:1.3]. On the night he said this, he was in fact preparing to lay down his own life. He also said that if the apostles loved one another with this love, all men would know that they were his disciples [180:1.1]. The new commandment calls for still greater acts of love within the kingdom of the believing brotherhood [180:1.1]. Jesus said he had chosen and ordained the apostles to go into the world and bear the fruit of loving service [180:1.4], and after the resurrection he urged John to learn to love men as he had loved him [192:2.1].

2. Not a Burden but a New Joy

Jesus said that this commandment does not place a new burden on the soul but brings a new joy, the joy of bestowing the affection of the heart upon one's fellows [180:1.2]. He himself, though outwardly enduring sorrow, was about to experience the supreme joy of bestowing that affection [180:1.2]. Those who follow this command will experience the fullness of divine joy [180:1.4].

3. A Relationship Not of Servants but of Friends

Jesus no longer called the apostles servants but friends, and said that they would continue to be his friends if only they loved one another [180:1.3]. The Urantia Book stresses that what Jesus demands is loyalty, not sacrifice [180:1.6]. The consciousness of sacrifice implies the absence of wholehearted affection, and the idea of duty signifies a servant mind [180:1.6]. So it says that "⟦Q 180:1.6⟧the service of a friend for a friend can never be called a sacrifice⟦/Q⟧" [180:1.6]. Jesus had taught them that they were the sons of God, had called them brethren, and before he left he called them his friends [180:1.6].

4. Love Shows Itself in Service and Makes the Old World New

To share the Master's joy we must share his love, and to share his love means to share his service [180:1.5]. This love does not deliver us from the difficulties of the world or create a new world, but "⟦Q 180:1.5⟧it most certainly does make the old world new⟦/Q⟧" [180:1.5]. In the same discourse Jesus said that even the golden rule, without the insight of the Spirit of Truth, is merely a rule of ethics [180:5.5], and that it can be understood only when lived out not as doctrine or precept but by the living interpretation of the Spirit of Truth [180:5.11]. The new commandment likewise is not a rule but a living relationship in which one who has experienced Jesus' love shares that love.

Summary

The old commandment says to love one's neighbor with oneself as the standard, but the new commandment takes as its standard the love with which Jesus loved us, the love that lays down its life for its friends [180:1.1, 180:1.3]. It is not a burden but a joy, not duty or sacrifice but the loyalty of a friend [180:1.2, 180:1.6], and it makes the old world new through mutual service [179:3.6, 180:1.5].

q336.question: What is the meaning of Jesus' praying three times about "this cup" in Gethsemane?
q336.answer:
The prayer in Gethsemane is the moment when Jesus' humanity was most deeply revealed and the moment when his human will became wholly one with the Father's will. The Urantia Book explains that before the greatest revelation of his divinity, the resurrection, there had to come first the greatest proof of his mortal nature, the humiliation and the crucifixion [182:3.5]. The three prayers show the process by which a human heart, seeking a way of escape, gradually accepted the Father's will [182:3.6, 182:3.9].

According to The Urantia Book's explanation, to drink that cup was to experience death as a mortal, not using his power to save himself but submitting to the natural course of events [182:3.6, 182:3.7].

1. The Course of the Three Prayers

In the first prayer Jesus said that he did not shrink from laying down his life in the flesh, and prayed to know whether it was the Father's will that he drink this cup [182:3.1]. In the second prayer he said he knew it was possible to avoid this cup, but that he would drink it if it was the Father's will, and then a mighty angel came down, touched him, and strengthened him [182:3.2]. In the third prayer, after asking mercy for the sleeping apostles, he ended: "⟦Q 182:3.4⟧Que no se haga mi voluntad, sino la tuya».⟦/Q⟧" [182:3.4]. With each prayer his humanity laid hold of his divinity with a more resolute faith, and his human will became increasingly one with the Father's will [182:3.6].

2. The Father's Will Conveyed by the Angel

One of the messages the mighty angel brought was that, just as all mortal creatures experience material dissolution in passing from time into eternity, the Father desired the Son to finish his earth bestowal by the creature experience of death [182:3.6]. Jesus was assured that the Father intended to allow natural events to run their course, and he fully decided not to use his sovereign power as the supreme head of the universe to save himself [182:3.7]. The celestial host assembled under the direction of Gabriel and the Personalized Adjuster was also warned not to interfere without his command [182:3.8].

3. The Human Causes of His Anguish

His anguish was not merely physical fear. He was exhausted from long labor and from anxiety for the safety of his apostles, and he endured such anguish that his sweat fell in great drops [182:3.7]. The sorrow of love at leaving his weak and ignorant apostles, his isolation from his family, the betrayal by a chosen associate, and the rejection by his own people came together, so that his soul suffered from frustrated love and rejected mercy [182:3.9]. His humanity was not insensible to personal loneliness, public shame, and the appearance of the failure of his cause [182:3.10]. He longed for them to watch with him, but the three apostles fell asleep again and again [182:3.2, 182:3.3].

4. The Recovery of Poise

He comforted himself and strengthened his mind with happy memories of Nazareth and Galilee [182:3.10], and before Judas and the soldiers arrived he had fully regained his customary poise: "⟦Q 182:3.11⟧the spirit had triumphed over the flesh; faith had asserted itself over all human tendencies to fear or entertain doubt⟦/Q⟧" [182:3.11]. He had passed the supreme test of the full realization of the human nature [182:3.11].

Summary

The three prayers in Gethsemane were a process that began with Jesus' human heart seeking a way of escape and ended in his wholehearted acceptance of the Father's will that he experience death as a mortal without using his sovereign power [182:3.6, 182:3.7]. That cup was bitter and painful, but he laid hold of his divinity by faith and regained his poise [182:3.11], and this shows that we too, in our sufferings, can seek the Father's will rather than our own [182:3.4].

q337.question: Why did Peter deny the Master three times, and how did Jesus restore him?
q337.answer:
Peter's denial was not a betrayal born of malice; it was a failure in which, in the midst of fear, he took one step onto the path of compromise and least resistance and then could not turn back from it [184:2.4, 184:2.12]. Unlike Judas, Peter sincerely loved the Master, and he was the first to make a full and public confession of Jesus' divinity [179:3.2]. So this story is also one that shows how a fallen believer rises again.

The Urantia Book recounts in detail how the denial came about, its causes, and the way the risen Master restored Peter.

1. He Was Where He Should Not Have Been

Peter was by the charcoal fire in the courtyard of Annas's palace, in the midst of Jesus' enemies, and The Urantia Book says that he had no business being there [184:2.2]. The Master had not asked him to stay near, as he had John, and the apostles had been specially warned not to endanger their lives during the trial and crucifixion [184:2.2]. His mind was filled with confusion, and he scarcely realized that Jesus had been arrested [184:2.3].

2. The Course of the Denials

When the portress mischievously questioned him, Peter was so tense that, with only the thought of escaping with his life, he answered, "I am not" [184:2.4]. When another servant asked, he vehemently denied any connection with Jesus [184:2.5], and when the portress pressed him again he cursed and swore that he did not know him [184:2.6]. When his Galilean accent was pointed out he denied it as well, and when he denied it yet again in the porch, the cock crowed [184:2.7, 184:2.8]. Up to that moment he had only been congratulating himself on having cleverly evaded the servants' accusations and did not realize that he had denied his Master [184:2.11]. By The Urantia Book's account, he denied him five times in all [184:2.4-2.8].

3. Why He Could Not Stop

The Urantia Book draws an important lesson here. Having taken the first step along the path of compromise, Peter could see nothing to do but go on with the course of conduct he had decided upon [184:2.12]. "⟦Q 184:2.12⟧Hace falta carácter magnánime y noble para retomar el camino recto después de haber empezado mal.⟦/Q⟧." [184:2.12] Once one has entered on the wrong path, the mind all too easily tends to keep justifying that choice [184:2.12].

4. The Master's Look and Peter's Tears

As Jesus was led past Peter on his way to Caiaphas, he saw the despairing apostle's face and turned and looked at him. It was a look blended of pity and love, and Peter never forgot that look as long as he lived [184:2.8]. Peter sat down by the roadside and wept bitterly [184:2.9]. But he could not fully believe that he could be forgiven until, after the resurrection, he met the Master and saw that he was received just as before [184:2.13].

5. The Risen Master's Restoration

On the evening of the resurrection day Jesus appeared to Peter in the garden of the Mark home. This was the eighth morontia manifestation, and Peter was struggling with the fear that he might no longer be an apostle [191:1.1]. The Master said, "⟦Q 191:1.2⟧I knew it was not from the heart that you disowned me⟦/Q⟧" [191:1.2], and told him that he had forgiven him even before he asked [191:1.2]. Peter rushed to the upper chamber and exclaimed that the Master had forgiven him [191:1.4]. Later, by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus asked Peter three times whether he loved him, and entrusted him with the charge to feed his lambs and to forgive his fellows as Jesus had forgiven him [192:2.2-2.4].

Summary

In fear and confusion Peter took the first step toward compromise and, while justifying that course, denied the Master more than three times [184:2.4-2.8, 184:2.12]. But the Master looked at him with a look of love, and after the resurrection told him he had forgiven him even before he asked, and entrusted the flock to him again [184:2.8, 191:1.2, 192:2.4]. More important than falling is rising again by that love.

q338.question: What words and attitude did Jesus show on the cross, and what does "My God, why have you forsaken me?" mean?
q338.answer:
The Urantia Book sums it up: "⟦Q 187:5.6⟧Jesus died royally—as he had lived⟦/Q⟧" [187:5.6]. He remained master of the situation throughout that tragic day, and the few words he spoke on the cross all reveal forgiveness, mercy, care, and trust in the Father [187:5.2, 187:5.6]. Even the so-called "cry of forsakenness" was not a confession of despair but a verse of a Psalm he was reciting in his mind [187:5.2].

Taking his words and attitude on the cross in order, we see the following.

1. A Prayer of Forgiveness for His Executioners

As the soldiers nailed him to the crossbeam, Jesus' only words were a prayer asking the Father to forgive them [187:2.4]. The Urantia Book says that he could not have interceded so mercifully had not thoughts of affectionate devotion been the mainspring of his whole life of unselfish service, and that "⟦Q 187:2.4⟧Las ideas, motivos y anhelos de toda una vida se revelan abiertamente en una crisis.⟦/Q⟧." [187:2.4] He also refused to drink the drugged wine offered to deaden the pain, after tasting it [187:2.3].

2. The Promise to the Repentant Brigand

When one brigand railed at Jesus, the other rebuked him and asked Jesus to remember him when he came into his kingdom [187:4.1]. Jesus smiled at him and promised that he would sometime be with him in Paradise [187:4.1]. Seeing the way Jesus met death, this brigand could no longer resist the conviction that he was truly the Son of God [187:4.2]. Had anyone in the jeering crowd appealed to him in faith, he would have been received with the same love [187:4.6].

3. Entrusting His Mother to John

At noon Jesus entrusted John to his mother Mary as her son and Mary to John as his mother, and told the two of them to leave the place [187:4.7]. Even at the moment of his own death he thought first of the future of those he loved. He said that he was thirsty, and the captain of the guard moistened his lips with a sponge soaked in sour wine [187:5.3].

4. The Meaning of "⟦Q 187:5.2⟧My God, Why Have You Forsaken Me?⟦/Q⟧"

Shortly after one o'clock, in the darkness of the sandstorm, Jesus, failing in consciousness, repeated in his mind passages of the twentieth, twenty-first, and twenty-second Psalms, and those standing by caught only a few of them [187:5.1, 187:5.2]. The Urantia Book makes it clear that Jesus did not for one moment doubt that he had lived according to the Father's will, and that "⟦Q 187:5.2⟧He did not feel that the Father had forsaken him⟦/Q⟧" [187:5.2]. Those words were the recitation of the first line of the twenty-second Psalm [187:5.2].

5. His Last Words and What Followed

Just before three o'clock Jesus cried out that it was finished and that he commended his spirit into the Father's hands, and then he breathed his last [187:5.5]. The Roman centurion who saw this said that this man must truly have been a Son of God, and from that time he began to believe [187:5.5]. Because of his overwhelming emotional anguish and spiritual suffering, his mortal life ended in less than five and a half hours [187:5.8]. When he breathed his last, John Zebedee, his brother Jude, his sister Ruth, Mary Magdalene, and others were at the foot of the cross [187:5.4]. Having lived such a life and died such a death, he could truly say that it was finished [187:5.6].

Summary

On the cross Jesus forgave his executioners, received the repentant brigand, cared for his mother, and committed his spirit to the Father [187:2.4, 187:4.1, 187:4.7, 187:5.5]. The "cry of forsakenness" was only the recitation of the twenty-second Psalm; he did not feel forsaken by the Father [187:5.2], and his death was the final expression of a life lived in love [187:5.6].

q339.question: Was Jesus' death on the cross an atonement paying for our sins in our place? What does The Urantia Book say is the true meaning of the cross?
q339.answer:
The Urantia Book answers plainly. Jesus did not die to atone for the guilt of mankind, to appease the wrath of God, or to pay a debt owed to God [188:4.1, 188:4.3]. But it says that the error of this atonement idea does not lessen the significance of the cross, and that we must also guard against the great mistake of missing the true meaning of the Master's death [188:4.1, 188:4.2]. The cross is not a price paid to satisfy God's demands; it is the revelation in which the Father's love, made manifest through the Son, reached its climax [188:5.11].

1. What The Urantia Book Denies: The Ideas of Ransom and Substitution

Mortals were never the possession of the deceivers, so Jesus had no need to pay a ransom to deliver them [188:4.3]. The Father in heaven has never harbored the injustice of condemning a mortal soul because of the evil-doing of its ancestors [188:4.3], and sin is not passed on from parents to children but is the conscious and deliberate rebellion of an individual will creature [188:4.5]. Once we grasp God as a true and loving Father, we must abandon the primitive notion of a stern ruler who withholds punishment only if someone else dies in our stead. "⟦Q 188:4.8⟧Toda la idea del rescate y de la expiación es incompatible con el concepto de Dios tal como lo enseñó y ejemplificó Jesús de Nazaret.⟦/Q⟧." [188:4.8] Even a monarch of strict law would not be satisfied with the childish device of substituting an innocent person for the sinner [188:4.11].

2. Why, Then, Did He Die?

Jesus chose to live a full mortal life on Urantia, and death is the final scene of that mortal drama [188:4.2]. His death contributed greatly to making forever plain the certainty of survival after death in the flesh [188:4.6]. So although it may not be proper to call him a redeemer or ransomer, it is wholly right to call him a savior [188:4.7]. What is important is not the fact of his death itself but "⟦Q 188:4.12⟧the superb manner and the matchless spirit in which he met death⟦/Q⟧" [188:4.12].

3. What the Cross Reveals

The cross forever places all relations between God and man on the family basis: God is the Father, and man is his son [188:5.1]. The cross shows that Jesus' attitude toward sinners was neither condemnation nor condonation but eternal and loving salvation, and divine love does not merely forgive wrongs but absorbs and actually destroys them [188:5.2]. By his prayer of forgiveness for his executioners he made the cross the eternal symbol of the triumph of love over hate [188:5.6]. He also had a love greater than any love yet known, a love great enough to lay down his life even for his enemies [188:5.7].

4. The Lesson for Our Lives

The idea of atonement salvation is rooted in selfishness, and the believer's chief concern should not be the desire for personal salvation but the urge to love and serve his fellows as Jesus did [188:4.9]. The cross is the symbol of holy service, the dedication of one's life to the welfare of one's fellows, and the symbol of the good giving themselves to the evil in order to save them [188:5.9]. One who looks upon it ceases to complain of the hardships of life [188:5.10] and can no longer fear that the Creator does not know his suffering [188:5.12]. The evolving creatures of countless worlds, too, have drawn inspiration to go on fighting the good fight of faith by looking upon Jesus on the cross [188:5.5].

Summary

The death on the cross was not a substitutionary atonement to appease God or pay a debt, nor was it designed to reconcile man to God [188:4.1, 188:5.13]. It was a revelation to bring men to an awareness of the Father's love and the Son's mercy [188:5.13]; "⟦Q 188:5.11⟧There was nothing in the cross which the Father required—only that which Jesus so willingly gave⟦/Q⟧" [188:5.11], the love he freely bestowed.

q340.question: Was Jesus' resurrection the coming back to life of his body? Please explain the relationship between the empty tomb and the morontia resurrection.
q340.answer:
According to The Urantia Book, Jesus' resurrection was not the reviving of his dead body but a resurrection in morontia form and personality. At two minutes past three o'clock on Sunday morning, April 9, A.D. 30, the resurrected morontia form and personality of Jesus came forth from the tomb, while his physical body still lay in the burial niche, wrapped in linen cloths [189:1.1, 189:1.2]. The empty tomb is a fact, but it is not the truth of the resurrection [189:2.6].

The Urantia Book offers three statements, saying it wishes to make this matter forever clear [189:1.6].

1. Three Key Statements about the Resurrection

First, his material body was not a part of the resurrected personality, and he came forth from the tomb without moving the stones and without disturbing Pilate's seals [189:1.7]. Second, he did not come forth as a spirit, nor as Michael of Nebadon in the form of the Creator sovereign he had been before the incarnation [189:1.8]. Third, he came forth as a morontia personality, in exactly the likeness in which resurrected ascenders appear in the resurrection halls of the first mansion world of Satania [189:1.9]. That is, Jesus experienced in advance the very resurrection that mortals experience on the mansion worlds after death.

2. Who Raised Him?

Seven Paradise personalities surrounded the tomb, but the revelators say they did not observe them doing anything in connection with the Master's awakening, and that no creature of this local universe took part [189:1.1, 189:1.5]. "⟦Q 189:1.13⟧And he has done all this through power inherent within himself⟦/Q⟧" [189:1.13]. The first thing the risen Jesus did was to greet Gabriel and leave the universe affairs in his charge, and he told the assembled morontia group from the mansion worlds that he would tarry a while in the transition form in order more fully to know the life of ascending creatures [189:1.10]. Having laid down his life as a mortal on Friday, he took it up again on Sunday morning as a morontia being of the system of Satania [189:1.4].

3. Why Was the Tomb Empty?

The chief of the archangels asked for authority to dissolve the body at once, so that the celestial hosts would not have to witness the slow decay of the Creator's human form, and permission was granted [189:2.1, 189:2.2]. Since the material body could not pass out of the sealed tomb as the morontia form had, the secondary midwayers rolled away the stones at the entrance, and the guards who saw this fled [189:2.3, 189:2.4]. The Jewish leaders bribed the guards to say that the disciples had taken the body away by night [189:2.5]. The tomb was empty not because the body had been revived but because the natural dissolution of "dust to dust" took place almost instantly, without the delays of time [189:2.7, 189:2.8].

4. Why This Distinction Matters

The first believers combined the fact of the empty tomb with the fact of the resurrection and formed the untrue belief that Jesus' material body had been raised [189:2.6]. The Urantia Book warns that "⟦Q 189:2.6⟧Although individual facts may be materially true⟦/Q⟧" [189:2.6], their combination does not necessarily lead to spiritually true conclusions. The true evidence of the resurrection is spiritual in nature, and the testimony of almost a thousand persons who met the risen Master supports it [189:2.9]. This teaching connects with the larger truth that matter is the skeleton of morontia, and that both are the shadows of spirit reality [189:1.3].

Summary

Jesus rose not in the flesh but as a morontia personality, by power inherent within himself [189:1.7, 189:1.9, 189:1.13]. The tomb was empty only because his body was dissolved almost instantly in the manner authorized for the celestial hosts [189:2.7], and this resurrection is the pattern of the resurrection every believer will experience on the mansion worlds after death [189:1.9].

q341.question: In what kind of body, to whom, and how many times did the risen Jesus appear, and what do those appearances show?
q341.answer:
The risen Jesus appeared in a morontia body, a transition form midway between the material and the spiritual. From his morontia resurrection to his spirit ascension, he made nineteen separate appearances in visible form to believers, and he did not appear to his enemies or to those who could not make spiritual use of the appearance [190:2.1]. These appearances show that the resurrection was a reality and not a vision, and what the morontia career that mortals will walk after death is like [190:0.1, 190:0.3].

The Urantia Book recounts in detail the order and places of the appearances and the character of the morontia body.

1. The Character of the Morontia Body

The mortals of the realms will also arise on the morning of the resurrection with the same type of morontia body that Jesus had when he arose from the tomb [190:0.3]. These bodies do not have circulating blood and do not partake of ordinary food; "⟦Q 190:0.3⟧nevertheless, these morontia forms are real⟦/Q⟧" [190:0.3]. What the believers saw was not a hallucination [190:0.3]. With the help of the morontia associate personalities, this form could at times become, like spirit, indifferent to matter, and at other times be discernible and contactable by mortals [189:2.3]. That is why Jesus could appear inside locked doors and vanish in an instant [191:2.1, 191:2.2].

2. The Course of the Appearances

The first and second appearances were at the tomb, to the five women and to Mary Magdalene [190:2.1]. The third was to his brother James at Bethany [190:2.2, 190:2.3], the fifth to the women at the home of Joseph, the sixth to the Greek believers, and the seventh to the two brothers on the way to Emmaus [190:3.1, 190:4.1, 190:5.2]. The eighth was to Peter and the ninth to the ten apostles in the upper chamber [191:1.1, 191:2.2], and then, by way of Philadelphia, Alexandria, the shore of the Sea of Galilee, the Mount of Ordination, Sychar, and Tyre [191:4.1, 191:6.1, 192:1.1, 192:3.1, 193:1.3, 193:2.1], the last appearance took place in Jerusalem on May 18 [193:3.1]. Mary Magdalene witnessed four of the first five appearances [190:3.2].

3. Forty Days of Experiencing the Morontia Career

The risen Jesus experienced on Urantia the ascending morontia career through which the mortals of the realms pass, corresponding to what the mortals of Satania experience on the seven mansion worlds [190:0.1]. More than a million morontia directors and associates were present, and for forty days he stayed with them, teaching and learning [191:3.1]. After he passed to the second stage of morontia progression, it became increasingly difficult to make him visible to mortal eyes [191:3.2].

4. Thomas's Doubt and "Those Who Have Not Seen and Yet Believe"

Thomas, who had spent a week alone, said that he would not believe unless he put his finger in the print of the nails [191:5.2]. When Jesus appeared, he said that there were no nail marks in his hands because he had been raised in the form that Thomas too would have when he left this world [191:5.4]. When Thomas knelt and confessed that he believed, Jesus said that those who believe without seeing with the eye of flesh are blessed [191:5.5]. Thomas's doubt asserted itself most stubbornly just when it was about to collapse, but he had already begun to believe in his heart [191:5.4]. These words are also spoken to later believers who do not see the appearances.

Summary

The risen Jesus appeared nineteen times to believers in a morontia body that has no flowing blood yet is real [190:0.3, 190:2.1]. These appearances bear witness to the reality of the resurrection and show that he first experienced the morontia career that mortals will walk on the mansion worlds in the future [190:0.1, 191:3.1]. And the gift of life he gave still guarantees the resurrection of believers today [190:0.2].

q342.question: How did Jesus' ascension take place, and what was his final charge to the apostles before he departed?
q342.answer:
According to The Urantia Book, the so-called ascension of Jesus took place on Thursday morning, May 18, on the western slope of the Mount of Olives, in the sight of the eleven apostles [193:5.1]. But it was not a dramatic spectacle of a body rising into the clouds; it was the morontia Master vanishing from their sight, in no way different from the other occasions on which he had vanished from mortal view during the forty days [193:5.3]. On the unseen level, the Master's spirit ascension and the confirmation of his sovereignty followed [193:5.4, 193:5.5].

The events before and after the ascension and the final charge can be summarized as follows.

1. The Last Appearance in the Upper Chamber in Jerusalem

That morning Jesus made his last morontia appearance on earth to the eleven apostles in the upper chamber of the home of Mary Mark [193:3.1]. He told them to tarry in Jerusalem until the Spirit of Truth was poured out upon all flesh and endowed them with power from on high [193:3.2]. When Simon Zelotes asked whether he would restore the kingdom, Jesus said that he still clung to his old ideas of a material kingdom, and told him that they would receive spiritual power and preach the gospel to all the world [193:3.2].

2. Trust and Confide in One Another

At the center of the final charge were the words to love and trust one another. Jesus said that Judas was no longer with them because his love had grown cold and he had refused to trust his loyal brethren [193:3.2]. He reminded them that he had sent them out two and two to keep them from the mischief of isolation, and that even when he communed with the Father he had always kept two or three of them by his side [193:3.2]. And he charged them: "⟦Q 193:3.2⟧Trust, therefore, and confide in one another⟦/Q⟧." [193:3.2] In his farewell message the Master held up the fate of Judas as a warning against the dangers of brotherly isolation [193:4.1].

3. The Farewell Words on the Mount of Olives

From the upper chamber to the Mount of Olives no one spoke a word, and when they reached the mount the apostles, without being instructed, knelt in a circle about him [193:3.3, 193:5.1]. Jesus told them to love men with the love with which he had loved them, and to serve their fellow mortals as he had served them [193:5.2]. He also told them to lead souls, by the spirit fruits of their lives, to believe the truth that man is a son of God and that all men are brethren, and he took his leave with the words: "⟦Q 193:5.2⟧My love overshadows you, my spirit will dwell with you, and my peace shall abide upon you⟦/Q⟧." [193:5.2]

4. The Unseen Journey of Ascension

The morontia Jesus vanished from the apostles' sight at about a quarter to eight in the morning and set out on his ascent to the right hand of the Father, there to receive formal confirmation of his completed sovereignty over Nebadon [193:5.5]. He went by way of Jerusem to Edentia, where the Most Highs released him from the morontia state and restored him to the status of Paradise sonship and the supreme sovereignty of Salvington [193:5.4]. This spirit ascension is counted as the sixth of the seven steps by which Jesus ascended from the human to the divine [196:1.6, 196:1.12].

5. The Disciples after the Ascension

Peter soon gathered some one hundred and twenty of the leading disciples and reported the last farewell and the ascension [193:6.1, 193:6.2], and the eleven apostles cast lots and installed Matthias in the place of Judas [193:6.3]. And they waited for the promised Spirit of Truth [193:5.2].

Summary

The ascension was the morontia Master vanishing from the apostles' sight on the Mount of Olives, after which he went by way of Edentia back to the sovereignty of Salvington [193:5.3, 193:5.4]. His final charge was to wait for the Spirit of Truth, to love and serve men as he had loved and served them, and to trust one another and not become isolated [193:3.2, 193:5.2].

q343.question: How does The Urantia Book diagnose modern materialism and secularism, and how should believers respond?
q343.answer:
After surveying the history of Christianity since Pentecost, Paper 195 names materialism and secularism as great problems of the modern world. The Urantia Book's diagnosis is clear. Materialism denies God, and secularism simply ignores him [195:8.5]; both confine man to the level of things and rob him of faith, hope, and eternal assurance [195:6.7], and in the end they cannot bring peace [195:8.6]. At the same time, however, it says that this panic is a passing episode and that the religion of Jesus has never gone bankrupt [195:6.1, 195:6.4].

This diagnosis does not deny science or secular achievement; it points out their limits when they try to stand alone without God.

1. The Problem of Materialism: It Makes Man a Machine

Scientists have unintentionally precipitated mankind into a materialistic panic, but only unthinking people panic about the spiritual assets of the human race [195:6.1]. Materialism makes man a soulless automaton [195:6.8]. But "⟦Q 195:6.11⟧A machine cannot know⟦/Q⟧" [195:6.11], much less know truth, hunger for righteousness, and cherish goodness [195:6.11]. The very existence of a self-conscious human who declares himself to be a machine is the best answer to mechanism [195:7.13]. Materialism exists, but it is not exclusive; determinism exists too, but it is not the only thing [195:6.14].

2. Science and Religion Do Not Quarrel

True religion cannot become involved in a controversy with science. Religion is not concerned with material things but is deeply concerned with the scientist [195:6.2]. Science is a quantitative experience and religion a qualitative one; science deals with phenomena, religion with origins, values, and goals [195:6.5]. Facts never clash with real spiritual faith, but theories may [195:7.1]. Science should do for man materially what religion does for him spiritually: extend the horizon of life and enlarge his personality [195:7.2].

3. The Problem of Secularism: No Brotherhood without God

The father of secularism was atheistic science and its mother the totalitarian medieval church, and it began as a protest against the domination of the church [195:8.2]. Secularism broke the fetters of the church, but it now threatens to set up a new godless domination, the totalitarian state [195:8.4]. The Urantia Book declares: "⟦Q 195:8.11⟧No se puede establecer la hermandad de los hombres si se ignora o niega la paternidad de Dios.⟦/Q⟧." [195:8.11] Yet it keeps a balance, saying that one need not abandon faith in order to enjoy the benefits of the secular revolt, namely tolerance, social service, democratic government, and civil liberties [195:8.8], and that those benefits should not be hastily thrown away either [195:8.6].

4. The Believer's Response

One of the great problems of modern times is that men think they are too busy to find time for spiritual meditation and religious devotion [195:6.7]. It is also an error for religious leaders to try to call modern man with the trumpet blasts of the Middle Ages; religion must provide itself with new slogans suited to the age [195:6.10]. The sincere pursuit of goodness, beauty, and truth leads to God [195:6.17], and if we have begun to seek God, that is proof that God has already found us [195:6.16]. When the materialistic sociologist leaves people just as he found them, the Galileans, having seen the life of Jesus, shook the Roman Empire [195:6.9].

Summary

The Urantia Book diagnoses that materialism tries to make man a machine and secularism tries to make a society without God, but that neither can give peace or a true brotherhood [195:6.8, 195:8.11, 195:8.12]. Believers should not fear science [195:6.2]; while keeping the benefits of secular achievement [195:8.8], they should show forth the living religion of Jesus in language suited to the age and in actual living [195:6.10, 195:6.1].

q344.question: What kind of faith is "the faith of Jesus" of which the last paper of The Urantia Book speaks, and what does it mean to follow him?
q344.answer:
The last paper of The Urantia Book deals not with faith in Jesus but with "the faith of Jesus," the faith that the human Jesus held toward God. He experienced all the ups and downs of mortal existence, yet he never religiously doubted the certainty of God's watchcare and guidance, and his faith was the outgrowth of the insight born of the activity of the indwelling Adjuster [196:0.1]. The Urantia Book says that Jesus' greatest contribution to human experience lay not in revealing many new ideas about God but in showing a new and higher type of living faith in God [196:0.3].

Let us look in turn at the characteristics of that faith and at what it means to follow it.

1. A Personal and Living Faith

Jesus' faith was neither traditional nor merely intellectual; "⟦Q 196:0.1⟧it was wholly personal and purely spiritual⟦/Q⟧" [196:0.1]. Theology may fix and dogmatize faith, but for Jesus faith was a living, original, and spontaneous sublime experience and a profound conviction [196:0.5]. It was not something he clung to as a consolation in difficulty or a compensation for despair; it was the serenity enjoyed in unquestioning trust in God [196:0.3]. Even in the face of apparent defeat and the threat of a disgraceful death, that faith did not waver [196:0.5].

2. A Balanced Faith without Fanaticism

Strong spiritual faith often runs into fanaticism and the exaggeration of the religious ego, but this was not so with Jesus [196:0.6]. His faith was in harmony with a keen awareness of personal honor, family love, social obligation, and economic necessity [196:0.7], and he was so self-forgetful that when called a good teacher he answered, why do you call me good? [196:0.9] The secret of his religious life was not leadings or visions but the consciousness of God's presence, gained through intelligent prayer and sincere worship, that is, through unbroken communion with God [196:0.10].

3. A Faith Childlike but Not Childish

Jesus trusted God as a child trusts his parent, and he believed in the fundamental goodness of the universe [196:0.11]. He combined the trusting optimism of a child with the intelligent courage of a mature adult, and his faith grew so high that it knew no fear [196:0.11]. So "⟦Q 196:0.12⟧Notwithstanding that Jesus' faith was childlike, it was in no sense childish⟦/Q⟧." [196:0.12] At the same time, with strong determination he overcame countless disappointments and difficulties [196:0.14].

4. What It Means to Follow Jesus

Rather than requiring his disciples to believe in him, Jesus asks them to believe with him, to believe what he believed and as he believed [196:0.13]. To "follow Jesus" means personally to share his religious faith and to enter into the spirit of his life of unselfish service for men [196:1.3]. The goal is not to imitate his outward life literally but to trust God as he trusted God and to believe in men as he believed in men [196:1.5]. The Urantia Book says that theological controversy must not obscure the religious man Jesus, who knew and did the will of God by faith, and that he was the most truly religious man who ever lived on Urantia [196:1.1]. And it foresees that if the theological religion about Jesus were replaced by the living religion of Jesus, the whole of civilization would be renewed [196:1.2].

Summary

The faith of Jesus was a trust born of the Adjuster's presence: personal and living, balanced and free of fanaticism, childlike but not childish [196:0.1, 196:0.7, 196:0.12]. To follow him is not to stop at worshiping him but to share his faith and to enter into the spirit of his life of serving men [196:0.13, 196:1.3, 196:1.5].
